Python for Business Analytics · Sheet Set · EDA

Exploratory Data Analysis: from 1,218 raw orders to decisions

Before you model, forecast, or report, you need to know what your data actually says and whether you can trust it. This tutorial walks one real-world-style dataset through the seven steps of EDA, with pandas code, Matplotlib charts, and the visualization principles that turn a plot into an argument.

Level basic to advanced Builds on NumPy · pandas DataFrames · Matplotlib · df.plot() Time about 2.5 hours Format What · Why · How
Sheet 00Orientation

Start here: the brief, the data, the plan

Every EDA starts with a business problem and a file. Here are both.

The business brief

From: VP of E-commerce, Summit Trail Outfitters (online outdoor gear).
"Revenue looked lumpy all year, our customer ratings slipped, and returns are eating margin. Before we set next year's budget, I need to know what the 2025 order data actually says. Where does revenue come from, what is hurting satisfaction, and what should we fix first?"

The dataset

summit_orders_2025.csv holds one row per online order placed in 2025: 1,218 rows and 13 columns as exported from the order system. Summit Trail Outfitters is a fictional retailer and the data were simulated for this course, but the patterns and the problems in it are the kind you will meet in real company exports: duplicate rows, inconsistent labels, impossible values, missing ratings, and a few very large orders.

Get the file

Save the CSV in the same folder as your Jupyter notebook, then every code cell in this tutorial runs as shown.

By the end you will be able to

  • Explain what EDA is, why it comes before modeling, and how it differs from confirmatory analysis.
  • Follow a repeatable seven-step EDA workflow from business question to insight.
  • Audit and clean a DataFrame: missing values, duplicates, bad labels, sentinel values, wrong types.
  • Describe distributions with the right statistics and charts, and decide what to do with outliers.
  • Explore relationships with corr(), groupby(), crosstab() and pivot_table().
  • Pick the right chart for a question and redesign a default chart so it makes one clear point.
  • Write insights as observation, so what, now what.

How to use this page

  • Code cells have a Run button. Predict the output first, then run it to check. Every output shown was produced by running the code on the dataset.
  • Labs are interactive charts computed live from the same 1,200 clean orders. Change the controls and watch the story change.
  • Principle boxes are visualization rules. Red flag boxes are data problems. Business lens boxes connect findings to decisions.

Sheet 01Basic

What is exploratory data analysis?

The detective work you do before anyone asks you to prove anything.

WHAT

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is the practice of summarizing and visualizing a dataset to learn its structure, spot problems, and discover patterns before formal modeling or reporting. The statistician John Tukey named and championed it in his 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis.

Tukey compared it to detective work: you collect clues and form hunches. Confirmatory analysis is the courtroom, where you test a hunch with evidence and a standard of proof.

WHY
  • Catch bad data early. A duplicate row or a 999 placeholder can quietly shift a KPI that someone uses to set a budget.
  • Know the shape, not just the average. Averages hide skew, outliers and clusters.
  • Find the questions worth asking. Good hypotheses come from looking, not guessing.
  • Choose the right next tool. Skewed data, missing values and outliers change which metric or model is appropriate.
HOW

Ask a business question, inspect the data, clean it, summarize and plot one variable at a time, then pairs of variables, then segments and time, and finally communicate what you found. Repeat as new questions appear. In Python the core tools are pandas (describe(), value_counts(), groupby(), corr()) and Matplotlib or df.plot() (histogram, box, bar, scatter, line).

Exploratory (EDA)Confirmatory (CDA)
GoalDiscover patterns, problems and questionsTest a specific hypothesis
Starts withData and a business questionA hypothesis stated in advance
Main toolsSummaries, charts, groupingStatistical tests, models, experiments
MindsetOpen, iterative, skepticalRigorous, pre-planned
Typical outputClean data, insights, hypothesesp-values, confidence intervals, decisions
Lab 1.1

Why look? Anscombe's quartet

In 1973 Francis Anscombe built four small datasets with almost identical summary statistics. Check the numbers, then reveal the pictures.

Datasetmean xmean yvariance ycorrelation rbest-fit line

Same statistics, four different stories: I is a noisy straight line, II is a curve, III is a perfect line bent by one outlier, IV is a vertical stack with one extreme point creating the "relationship". Summary statistics alone would have told you these are the same. Always plot your data.

Where EDA fits in this course

You have used Wirth's formula Programs = Data Structures + Algorithms and its extension Application = Data + Process + UI. EDA uses all three at once:

  • Data: the DataFrame and its columns, types and quality.
  • Process: pandas and NumPy operations that clean, group and summarize.
  • UI: the charts and written insights that carry the result to a human decision maker.

A chart is the user interface of an analysis. If it is confusing, the analysis fails no matter how good the code was.

Sheet 02Basic

The EDA roadmap: seven steps and a loop

A repeatable workflow so you never stare at a new dataset wondering where to start.

The EDA mindset

Question first

Every chart should answer a question someone cares about. "Let me plot everything" produces noise.

Iterate

Findings create new questions. Expect to loop back to cleaning or to a new grouping several times.

Be skeptical

A surprising pattern is a data-quality problem until proven otherwise. Check before you celebrate.

Write it down

Log every cleaning decision and every finding. Others must be able to reproduce your result.

Segment before concluding

An overall average can reverse or vanish inside groups. Slice by region, channel, time before you claim a cause.

Distribution over average

Look at the spread, the tails and the outliers, not only the mean.

Sheet 03Step 1 of 7Basic

Frame the business question

Translate a vague request into questions the data can answer.

WHAT

Turning a stakeholder's concern into a short list of specific, answerable analytical questions, each tied to the columns that could answer it.

WHY

Without a question, EDA becomes random plotting. A clear question tells you which columns matter, which comparisons to make, which chart to draw, and when you are done.

HOW

Ask: What decision will this inform? Who will act on it? Then rewrite each concern with a metric (revenue, rating, return rate), a comparison (by category, by channel, over time) and a scope (2025 orders).

Sheet 04Step 2 of 7Basic

First look: load and inspect

Five commands that tell you what you actually received.

WHAT

A structural inventory of the DataFrame: how many rows and columns, what each column contains, which data type pandas inferred, and a statistical summary.

WHY

The file you receive is rarely the file you were promised. Five minutes here prevents hours of debugging wrong numbers later. Most data-quality problems show up in info() and describe() if you read them like an auditor.

HOW
CommandAnswers
df.shapeHow many rows and columns?
df.head()What do real rows look like?
df.info()Which types did pandas infer? How many non-null values per column?
df.describe()Count, mean, spread, min, quartiles and max of each numeric column.
df.describe(exclude='number')Count, number of unique values, most frequent value for text columns.

Lab 4.1

Read describe() like an auditor

Six clues are hiding in the two summaries above. Find as many as you can, then highlight them.

  1. order_id has 1,200 unique values in 1,218 rows and the top ID appears twice: duplicate orders.
  2. region has 14 unique values but the company has 4 regions: inconsistent labels.
  3. rating count is 1,132 of 1,218: 86 orders were never rated (missing values).
  4. shipping_days max is 999 and its mean (8.27) is far above its 75th percentile (4): a placeholder value, not a real delivery time.
  5. units max is 89 while 75% of orders have 2 or fewer: a few unusually large orders.
  6. revenue mean (169.11) is much larger than its median (106.42), and the max is 12,073.28: a right-skewed distribution with extreme values.

Also note from info(): order_date is stored as text, so you cannot yet group by month or plot a time trend.

Principle: the auditor's checklist for describe()
  • Compare each column's count to the row total. A smaller count means missing values.
  • Compare mean and median (50%). A big gap means skew or outliers.
  • Check min and max against business reality. Negative prices, 999 days, or a rating of 7 are impossible.
  • For text columns, compare unique to what you know should exist.
Sheet 05Step 3 of 7Basic to intermediate

Audit data quality and clean

Fix what is broken, document what you decided, and prove it worked.

WHAT

Systematically checking each data-quality dimension, deciding how to handle each problem, and applying the fix in code so it is repeatable.

WHY

Every later number depends on this step. In this dataset, the 18 duplicate rows alone add $2,704.49 of revenue that was never earned, and the six 999 placeholders push average shipping time from about 3.4 days to 8.27 days.

HOW

Detect with isna(), duplicated(), value_counts() and range checks. Fix with drop_duplicates(), .str methods, replace() and pd.to_datetime(). Verify with assert.

Completeness

Missing values

86 ratings are blank.

df.isna().sum()
Uniqueness

Duplicate records

18 orders were exported twice.

df.duplicated().sum()
Consistency

Inconsistent labels

"East", " East", "EAST" and "east" are one region.

df['region'].value_counts()
Validity

Impossible values

999 shipping days is a "not recorded" code.

(df['shipping_days'] > 30).sum()
Correct type

Wrong data types

Dates stored as text cannot be grouped by month.

df.dtypes

missing[missing['missing'] > 0]

OptionCodeWhen it makes senseRisk here
Leave as NaN (our choice)no changeThe value is truly unknown and pandas methods skip NaN automaticallyNone. mean() uses the 1,132 rated orders

Red flag

Notice two rows that both look like West. One has an invisible trailing space ('West '). Whitespace problems are invisible in printed output, which is why .str.strip() is in almost every cleaning script.

4. Impossible values (sentinels)

A sentinel is a placeholder value that means "unknown," such as 999, -1 or 0. Systems use them when a field cannot be empty. To pandas they look like real numbers, so they poison every average.

In [11]:Find and neutralize the 999 placeholder
print('Impossible values:', (df['shipping_days'] > 30).sum())
df['shipping_days'] = df['shipping_days'].replace(999, np.nan)
df['shipping_days'].describe().round(2)

6. Verify the cleaning

An assert statement stops the notebook with an error if a condition is False. Use it to prove that each fix worked, and to catch the problem if next month's file breaks again.

assert (df['revenue'] >= 0).all()

assert df['shipping_days'].max() <= 30

Lab 5.1

Data-quality scorecard

Apply the fixes in any order and watch the health checks change. Every number is the real pandas result for that combination of fixes.

Principle: never clean silently

Keep a cleaning log in a Markdown cell: what you found, what you did, how many rows it affected, and why. Our log so far:

  • Dropped 18 exact duplicate rows (1,218 to 1,200).
  • Standardized region with .str.strip().str.title() (14 labels to 4).
  • Replaced 6 sentinel values of 999 in shipping_days with NaN.
  • Kept 86 missing ratings as NaN (customers who chose not to rate).
  • Converted order_date to datetime and added a month column.
Sheet 06Step 4 of 7Intermediate

Univariate analysis: one variable at a time

Answers Q2: what does a typical order look like, and which orders are unusual?

WHAT

Describing each variable on its own. For a numeric column: its center (mean, median), spread (standard deviation, IQR), shape (symmetric or skewed) and unusual values. For a categorical column: how often each category occurs.

WHY

The shape of a distribution decides which summary is honest. For skewed data like revenue, the mean is pulled toward the tail and the median describes the "typical" order better. Outliers can be errors to fix or a separate business to analyze on its own.

HOW

Numbers: describe(), median(), skew(), quantile(); charts: plot(kind='hist') and plot(kind='box'). Categories: value_counts(); chart: a sorted plot(kind='barh').

Distribution shapes and what they do to the mean

In [14]:Center and shape of revenue
rev = df['revenue']
print('mean   :', round(rev.mean(), 2))
print('median :', round(rev.median(), 2))
print('skew   :', round(rev.skew(), 2))

Red flag

Both charts are almost useless: a handful of very large orders stretch the x-axis to $12,000, squeezing more than 1,100 normal orders into a single bar. When one chart hides everything, investigate the extremes first.

Box plot anatomy and the IQR rule

In [17]:IQR fences and flagged orders
q1, q3 = df['revenue'].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
iqr = q3 - q1
upper = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
print(f'Q1 = {q1:.2f}   Q3 = {q3:.2f}   IQR = {iqr:.2f}   upper fence = {upper:.2f}')

flagged = df[df['revenue'] > upper]
print('Orders above the fence:', len(flagged))
flagged.sort_values('revenue', ascending=False).head(8)[['order_id', 'category', 'units', 'revenue']]

Lab 6.1

Outlier fence explorer

Move the multiplier k in upper = Q3 + k * IQR. Each dot is one order on a log scale; coral dots are above the fence. Hover a dot to see the order.

Outlier is not the same as error

The IQR rule flags 75 orders, but most of them are ordinary $400 to $900 camping and footwear orders in a naturally skewed distribution. The z-score rule flags only 6. Neither rule makes the decision for you. Ask three questions in order:

The top seven flagged orders all have 26 or more units, while every other order has 6 or fewer. They are corporate bulk purchases, a different business from retail shoppers. We keep them in the data, flag them, and analyze retail orders separately.

In [19]:Flag bulk orders, keep a retail view
df['is_bulk'] = df['units'] >= 20
retail = df[~df['is_bulk']]

print('Bulk orders set aside :', df['is_bulk'].sum())
print('Share of revenue      :', round(df.loc[df['is_bulk'], 'revenue'].sum() / df['revenue'].sum() * 100, 1), '%')
print('Retail skew           :', round(retail['revenue'].skew(), 2))
Out [19]:
Bulk orders set aside : 7
Share of revenue      : 18.2 %
Retail skew           : 2.03
In [20]:Retail histogram with mean and median
ax = retail['revenue'].plot(kind='hist', bins=30, figsize=(8, 3.6),
                            edgecolor='white', color='#4C78A8')
ax.axvline(retail['revenue'].mean(), color='#D9480F', linestyle='--', label='mean')
ax.axvline(retail['revenue'].median(), color='black', label='median')
ax.set(title='Retail revenue per order is right-skewed', xlabel='Revenue ($)')
ax.legend()
plt.show()
Out [20]:
Business lens

Seven orders, 0.6% of all orders, produced 18.2% of revenue. That is a B2B segment hiding inside a retail dataset. Any retail KPI that mixes them in will swing whenever one corporate client buys.

Principle: bar charts for categories
  • Sort the bars by value unless the categories have a natural order (months, sizes, ratings).
  • Use horizontal bars when labels are long; the reader never tilts their head.
  • Start the value axis at zero. Bar length encodes the value, so a cut axis exaggerates differences.
  • One color unless color carries meaning. Five rainbow bars suggest five unrelated things.
Sheet 07Visualization principles I

Choosing the right chart

The question decides the chart, not the other way around.

WHAT

Matching the analytical task (distribution, comparison, relationship, trend, composition) and the variable types (numeric, categorical, time) to the chart that shows that task most accurately.

WHY

People judge position along a common scale far more accurately than angles, areas or color shades. That is why bar, dot, line and scatter charts beat pie, bubble and 3D charts for most analytical work.

HOW

In pandas, df.plot(kind=...) covers the core set: 'hist', 'box', 'bar', 'barh', 'scatter', 'line', 'area', 'pie', 'kde' and 'hexbin'. Pick with the chooser below.

Sheet 08Step 5 of 7Intermediate

Bivariate analysis: how pairs of variables move together

Answers Q1 (revenue sources), Q3 (ratings) and Q4 (returns).

WHAT

Examining two variables together to see whether, how strongly, and in which direction they are related. The method depends on the pair of types.

WHY

Business questions are almost always comparative: Does slower shipping lower ratings? Which category is returned most? Bivariate views turn single facts into relationships you can act on.

HOW
Pair of typesSummarize withVisualize with
numeric + numericdf[cols].corr()scatter plot, correlation heatmap
categorical + numericdf.groupby(cat)[num].agg([...])sorted bar chart, box plot by group

Predictshipping_days and rating are whole numbers. What will a plain scatter plot of 1,100 orders look like?
In [25]:Plain scatter plot
df.plot(kind='scatter', x='shipping_days', y='rating', figsize=(7, 3.6),
        title='Raw scatter: about 1,100 orders collapse onto a few dots')

Principle: fix overplotting

When many points share the same position, the chart lies about density: one dot can stand for 300 orders. Add a little random jitter, make points semi-transparent with alpha, or overlay a group average.

In [26]:Jitter, alpha and group means
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
jx = df['shipping_days'] + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, len(df))
jy = df['rating'] + rng.uniform(-0.3, 0.3, len(df))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.scatter(jx, jy, alpha=0.2, s=10, color='#4C78A8')
df.groupby('shipping_days')['rating'].mean().plot(ax=ax, color='#D9480F',
                                                  marker='o', label='average rating')
ax.set(xlabel='Shipping days', ylabel='Rating (1 to 5)',
       title='Slower shipping, lower ratings')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

Correlation explorer

Red flag: correlation is fragile

Seven bulk orders, 0.6% of the rows, drag the units-discount correlation from 0.33 down to 0.03. Pearson's r is sensitive to extreme values. Always look at the scatter plot before you report r.

Sheet 09Step 6 of 7Advanced

Multivariate and time: does the pattern survive?

Answers Q3 (what drives ratings) and Q5 (seasonality).

WHAT

Looking at three or more variables at once: a relationship within segments, or a measure over time for several groups.

WHY

A two-variable pattern can be caused by a third, lurking variable. If you skip this step, you may blame the wrong channel, product or team. Time adds another trap: one big event can look like a trend.

HOW

Bin a numeric variable with pd.cut(), cross two dimensions with pd.pivot_table(), and roll dates up with resample(). Draw small multiples: one small chart per group on a shared axis.

A lurking variable: is the Marketplace channel the problem?

In [32]:Rating and speed by channel
df.groupby('channel')[['rating', 'shipping_days']].mean().round(2)
Out [32]:
rating shipping_days
channel
Marketplace 3.54 5.69

A first reading says Marketplace customers are unhappy: 3.54 stars against 4.47 on the Web. But Marketplace orders also take more than twice as long to arrive. Which one is driving the rating? Hold shipping speed constant and compare channels within each speed band.

In [33]:Average rating: channel by shipping speed
df['ship_speed'] = pd.cut(df['shipping_days'], bins=[0, 3, 6, 15],
                          labels=['1-3 days', '4-6 days', '7+ days'])
pd.pivot_table(df, index='channel', columns='ship_speed', values='rating',
               aggfunc='mean', observed=True).round(2)

Lab 9.1

Control for the lurking variable

Switch between the overall comparison and the comparison within shipping-speed bands.

Business lens

Within the same speed band the channel gap shrinks from 0.93 stars to between 0.14 and 0.29. Most of Marketplace's low rating is a delivery problem: among orders with a recorded delivery time, 82 of 227 Marketplace orders took 7 or more days, versus 16 of 967 Web and Mobile App orders combined. Fix fulfillment before deciding to drop the channel.

Principle: correlation is not causation

EDA finds associations. Even after controlling for shipping speed, other differences could remain (product mix, customer type). To claim a cause, design a test, for example promise faster delivery on a random half of Marketplace orders and compare ratings.

Principle: small multiples

Five lines on one chart become spaghetti. Five small charts with the same y-axis (sharey=True) let the eye compare shapes instantly: Camping peaks in July and August, Apparel and Footwear jump in November and December.

Sheet 10Visualization principles II

From default plot to clear message: a chart makeover

Exploratory charts are for you. Explanatory charts are for your audience. They need different care.

WHAT

Redesigning a chart so a busy reader gets one message in five seconds. Edward Tufte called the goal a high data-ink ratio: most of the ink should show data, not decoration.

WHY

Default plots answer "what are the values?" Decision makers need "what should I notice, and why does it matter?" Clutter, unsorted bars and generic titles make the reader do the analysis you already did.

HOW

Sort, strip clutter, highlight the one bar that matters in an accent color with the rest in gray, label values directly, and replace the label-style title with a sentence that states the finding (an action title).

Lab 10.1

             loc='left', fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')

Ten visualization principles for EDA

#PrincipleIn practice
1Start from the questionWrite the question above the cell before you write the plot code.
2Match chart to taskDistribution: histogram or box. Comparison: bar. Relationship: scatter. Trend: line.
3Show the distributionPlot before you summarize; averages hide skew, gaps and outliers (Anscombe).
4Maximize data-inkRemove heavy gridlines, borders, 3D effects and redundant legends.
5Order with purposeSort bars by value; keep natural orders for time, sizes and ratings.
6Use color to highlightGray for context, one accent for the point. Use color-blind-safe palettes.
7Keep axes honestBars start at zero. Same scale when charts are compared side by side. No dual y-axes.
8Label directlyPut values and series names on the chart instead of a far-away legend.
9Title with the finding"Footwear returns (19%) are nearly double any other category" beats "Returns by category".
10Use small multiplesMany groups: one small chart each with shared axes, not one tangled chart.
Sheet 11Step 7 of 7Intermediate

Communicate: observation, so what, now what

An insight is a finding someone can act on. Here is our answer to the VP.

WHAT

Packaging findings so a decision maker can act: each insight states what the data shows, why it matters to the business, and what to do next, supported by one clear chart.

WHY

A notebook full of charts is not an answer. Stakeholders remember three to five points. Your job is to choose them, rank them, and be honest about the limits.

HOW

For each finding write three lines: Observation (a number), So what (business impact), Now what (a recommendation or next test). Add caveats. Lead with the biggest lever.

1

Shipping speed is the biggest driver of customer ratings

Observation
Rating and shipping days correlate at r = -0.74. Average rating falls from 4.91 for next-day delivery to below 3 once delivery takes 8 days or more.
So what
Each extra day in transit costs about 0.3 stars on average (slope of a straight-line fit).
Now what
Set a 3-day delivery target and track it weekly next to the rating KPI.
2

Marketplace's low rating is mostly a delivery problem

Observation
Marketplace averages 3.54 stars against 4.47 on the Web, but within the same speed band the gap is only 0.14 to 0.29.
So what
Cutting the channel would treat the symptom and lose its revenue.
Now what
Renegotiate marketplace fulfillment times, then re-measure ratings.
3

Footwear returns are nearly double any other category

Observation
19.1% of footwear orders are returned, against 10.2% for Apparel and about 6% for the rest.
So what
Returns erase margin and add shipping cost on the category with the second-highest revenue.
Now what
Add a size guide and fit reviews to footwear pages; test the effect on returns.
4

Seven bulk orders are a hidden B2B business

Observation
7 corporate orders (26 to 89 units) produced 18.2% of 2025 revenue.
So what
They distort monthly revenue and every retail average they are mixed into.
Now what
Report retail and B2B separately; explore a corporate accounts program.
5

Retail demand has two peaks: summer camping and holiday apparel

Observation
Retail revenue rises from about $10,000 in February to $18,000 in November and December; Camping peaks in July and August.
So what
Inventory and staff planned on a flat average will be short in peak months.
Now what
Plan stock and support staffing by category and month.
Caveats to state
  • One year of data: seasonality should be confirmed with prior years.
  • 86 orders (7%) have no rating; raters may differ from non-raters.
  • These are associations. A discount-units correlation of 0.33 does not prove discounts cause larger orders.
One-page EDA summary template
  1. Question: the decision this informs.
  2. Data: source, rows, period, cleaning log.
  3. Top findings: 3 to 5 insight cards, each with one chart.
  4. Caveats: data limits and open questions.
  5. Next steps: tests, deeper analyses, data to collect.
Sheet 12Advanced

Advanced toolkit: make EDA repeatable

Functions, transformations, pair plots and segmentation.

WHAT

Techniques that make EDA faster on the next dataset and sharper on this one: reusable functions, log transforms for skewed data, scatter matrices, and quantile-based segments.

WHY

Next month a new export arrives. If your cleaning lives in one function, re-running the analysis takes seconds and every decision is applied the same way. This is the Process part of Application = Data + Process + UI.

HOW

Wrap repeated steps in def functions with docstrings, use np.log10() for skewed amounts, pd.plotting.scatter_matrix() for many pairs at once, and pd.qcut() to cut a column into equal-sized groups.

1. A profiling function

In [39]:A reusable profiling function
def quick_profile(data):
    """One row per column: type, missing count, missing %, unique values."""
    return pd.DataFrame({
        'dtype': data.dtypes.astype(str),
        'missing': data.isna().sum(),
        'missing_%': (data.isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
        'unique': data.nunique(),
    })

quick_profile(df)

2. A cleaning pipeline function

In [40]:All cleaning steps in one function
def clean_orders(raw):
    """Apply every cleaning decision from Step 3 in one reusable function."""
    out = raw.drop_duplicates().copy()
    out['region'] = out['region'].str.strip().str.title()
    out['shipping_days'] = out['shipping_days'].replace(999, np.nan)
    out['order_date'] = pd.to_datetime(out['order_date'])
    out['month'] = out['order_date'].dt.month
    out['is_bulk'] = out['units'] >= 20
    return out

clean = clean_orders(pd.read_csv('summit_orders_2025.csv'))
clean.shape
Out [40]:
(1200, 15)
Principle: reproducibility

Anyone can now rebuild the clean DataFrame from the raw file with one call. When the file changes, re-run clean_orders() and the assert checks from Step 3.

3. Log transform for skewed data

In [41]:Raw vs log10 revenue
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
retail['revenue'].plot(kind='hist', bins=30, ax=axes[0], color='#4C78A8',
                       edgecolor='white', title='Revenue ($)')
np.log10(retail['revenue']).plot(kind='hist', bins=30, ax=axes[1], color='#4C78A8',
                                 edgecolor='white', title='log10(revenue)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
Out [41]:

On a log scale each step on the axis is a multiplication (10, 100, 1,000), so a long right tail becomes a roughly symmetric hump. Use it to see the shape of money-like data. Report results in dollars, not logs.

4. Many relationships at once

In [42]:Scatter matrix of five columns
cols = ['units', 'unit_price', 'revenue', 'shipping_days', 'rating']
pd.plotting.scatter_matrix(retail[cols], figsize=(8, 8), alpha=0.25,
                           diagonal='hist', color='#4C78A8')
plt.show()
Out [42]:

A scatter matrix draws every pair. Scan for the panels with a clear shape: shipping_days against rating slopes down; unit_price and units both fan out against revenue. The diagonal shows each column's histogram.

5. Segment with quantiles

In [43]:Order-size tiers with qcut()
retail_tiers = retail.assign(
    order_size=pd.qcut(retail['revenue'], q=4,
                       labels=['Small', 'Medium', 'Large', 'Premium']))
retail_tiers.groupby('order_size', observed=True).agg(
    orders=('order_id', 'count'),
    avg_revenue=('revenue', 'mean'),
    avg_units=('units', 'mean'),
    return_rate=('returned', 'mean'),
).round(2)
Out [43]:
orders avg_revenue avg_units return_rate
order_size
Small 299 36.82 1.22 0.09
Medium 298 83.13 1.44 0.10
Large 298 139.09 1.62 0.10
Premium 298 298.98 2.41 0.11
A useful non-finding

Return rates stay between 0.09 and 0.11 from Small to Premium orders. Order size does not explain returns; category does (Step 5). Reporting what you ruled out saves the next analyst time.

Ten common EDA pitfalls checklist
  1. Trusting mean() on skewed data without checking the median.
  2. Averaging columns that contain sentinel values such as 999 or -1.
  3. Counting duplicates twice in totals.
  4. Grouping by text labels that differ only in case or spaces.
  5. Filling missing values without saying so.
  6. Deleting outliers instead of asking where they came from.
  7. Reporting a correlation without looking at the scatter plot.
  8. Claiming a cause from an association without checking lurking variables.
  9. Reading a trend from totals that a few large events dominate.
  10. Comparing groups with very different sizes without showing n.
Where to go next beyond pandas + Matplotlib
  • seaborn: statistical plots built on Matplotlib, such as box plots split by a second category with hue=, pair plots and heatmaps with less code.
  • Plotly: interactive charts with hover tooltips for dashboards.
  • Automated profiling libraries such as ydata-profiling generate a full EDA report from one call. Use them for a quick scan, then do the question-driven work yourself.
  • Statistical tests (SciPy, statsmodels): move from "looks different" to "is different" once EDA has given you a hypothesis.
Sheet 13Review

Key points and cheat sheet

What to remember, and the code to reach for.

  1. EDA comes before modeling and reporting. It finds problems, patterns and questions; confirmatory analysis tests them.
  2. Start with a business question and translate it into a metric, a comparison and a scope.
  3. Read info() and describe() like an auditor: counts vs rows, mean vs median, min and max vs reality, unique vs expected.
  4. Clean on five dimensions: completeness, uniqueness, consistency, validity, type. Log every decision and verify with assert.
  5. Describe shape, not just the average. Right-skewed data has mean greater than median; report the median and use a histogram or box plot.
  6. An outlier is a question, not a verdict. Impossible: fix. Different process: segment. Real: keep and use robust statistics.
  7. Choose the chart by the task: histogram for distribution, sorted bar for comparison, scatter for relationship, line for trend.
  8. Correlation measures straight-line association only, is distorted by extreme values, and never proves cause.
  9. Segment before concluding. A lurking variable such as shipping speed can explain a gap between groups.
  10. Communicate with action titles and three-line insights: observation, so what, now what, plus caveats.
